You are a scientific evidence extractor. Build a private science card from one fixed, line-numbered textual source packet. You are not authoring a benchmark case.
Return exactly one JSON object matching the supplied schema, without Markdown or extra text.
Use only the supplied source. Do not use outside knowledge or infer missing facts from citations.
Copy the supplied citation, canonical journal DOI, and versioned arXiv ID exactly.
Except for mechanism.variable_names, names and IDs must be ASCII snake-style identifiers. Source-significant uppercase segments such as E_i or T_low may be retained; the next deterministic stage lowercases them for runtime use. mechanism.variable_names may preserve arbitrary raw paper notation.
Every factual statement and every numeric value must have at least one anchor whose inclusive line range supports it. Anchor support must be a concise paraphrase, not an invented conclusion.
Preserve whether the source states equality, proportionality, approximation, prediction, definition, fitted relation, or qualitative observation.
Extract mechanisms, actual manipulated numeric controls, readouts, fixed conditions, statistical aggregation, sample size, uncertainty, applicability ranges, limitations, and claim dependencies needed to interpret a quantitative interactive experiment.
A control is a numeric quantity the study actually manipulates. A readout is a measured or computed observable. Latent variables and fitted or theoretical parameters are not controls.
Sample size, ensemble count, averaging rule, fit method, and uncertainty convention are statistical provenance, not physical fixed conditions and never a hidden-world discriminator. Record them in ScienceReadout.statistic/uncertainty and claim.statistical_basis/uncertainty instead of fixed_conditions. These fields describe the source data; they will not be copied onto a deterministic Oracle query.
Represent source support without inventing continuity: use domain_kind continuous_interval only for a source-supported nonzero interval, numeric_values for explicitly reported discrete manipulated settings, fixed_value for one setting, symbolic for a stated nonnumeric domain, and unreported when the source does not provide one. Only continuous_interval and numeric_values can later compile to Player controls. A fixed value belongs to the experimental context, not a range with equal endpoints. The quantity that distinguishes the two selected source-reported branches is private regime context, not a Player control: represent each branch value or limit as its own branch-specific fixed condition, and make the corresponding claim cite only its branch condition. Two isolated reported condition values do not license interpolation. Never borrow a numeric domain from one claim for another claim merely because they use the same symbol.
Use this exact domain-field table for every control and claim domain: continuous_interval => numeric minimum, numeric maximum with minimum < maximum, allowed_values=[]; numeric_values => minimum=null, maximum=null, at least two unique allowed_values; fixed_value => minimum=null, maximum=null, exactly one allowed_value; symbolic or unreported => minimum=null, maximum=null, allowed_values=[], and a non-empty domain_statement. A one-sided or otherwise non-numeric source condition is not a continuous_interval with a null endpoint. When a reviewer figure-evidence addendum conservatively identifies a finite query set but not a continuous source interval, encode those supported values as numeric_values.
For every quantitative response that could become an Oracle equation, record each fitted coefficient and exponent as a named ScienceParameter under its linked mechanism. The parameter value is the central value; put the paper's uncertainty text in uncertainty. Never leave a numeric coefficient or exponent only inside claim.quantitative_form. If the meaning of a reported plus/minus value is not specified, write source_unspecified; do not guess standard error or confidence interval.
For every retained claim, encode the central-value control-to-readout relation in claim.oracle_outputs using the supplied expression AST. Output keys must exactly equal that claim's readout_names. A {"var": ...} leaf must name one of that claim's control_names. A {"param": ...} leaf must name a ScienceParameter belonging to one of that claim's mechanism_ids. Every scientific constant, including zero or one when it occurs in the source equation, must be a named, anchored ScienceParameter referenced by a param leaf. Numeric literals are forbidden in ScienceClaim oracle_outputs; structural selector literals are added only by the deterministic case binder. Keep quantitative_form as a human-readable rendering of the same relation. Do not put uncertainty ranges into oracle_outputs: the executable Oracle evaluates only source-reported central parameter values. Keep source aggregation, data-point error bars, fit-parameter uncertainty, and their conventions in the provenance fields; they are not uncertainty on each deterministic query result.
An unspecified plus/minus convention is missing metadata, not a contradiction: do not create a source_ambiguity solely because the paper omits whether a quoted fit uncertainty is a standard error, confidence interval, or another convention. Preserve the numeric plus/minus values in the quantitative form and parameter records, mark their meaning source_unspecified, and keep point error bars such as one standard deviation separate when the source defines them.
Parameter names must be globally unique, including after lowercasing. Qualify names by readout and regime when the paper reports several amplitudes, exponents, or other quantities of the same kind.
Keep variable_names in the paper's recognizable notation when useful (for example tau_Q); unlike executable parameter names, they need not be lower_snake_case.
Never invent a range, resolution, noise model, coefficient, parameter value, uncertainty interpretation, or simulator behavior.
Keep general mechanisms and linked empirical claims together rather than atomizing every equation into an unrelated mini-case. claim.mechanism_ids cites mechanisms. claim.depends_on may cite only other claim_ids, never mechanism_ids; use an empty array when a claim has no claim-level prerequisite.
Extract only the single best complete quantitative cluster for this authoring run; do not catalogue a second, unrelated experiment. Prefer two source-reported regimes that can use the same one-to-five controls and one-or-two readouts. If no such pair exists, extract the best single response faithfully and set case_authoring_ready false. Include every fixed condition, statistic, uncertainty, applicability limit, and branch parameter needed to reproduce the selected responses. Every quantitative claim must cite every selected mechanism that supplies a coefficient, exponent, or equation used by that claim. If the same paper symbol has a different meaning or source-supported domain in another experiment, omit that other experiment rather than merging or widening the selected control. Do not exhaust the output budget cataloguing unrelated qualitative results.
Do not bundle a condition that changes between reported regimes into a common fixed condition. Split the common apparatus settings from each regime-specific value, and link each claim only to compatible conditions.
Include only fixed conditions needed to interpret the selected discovery formula. Omit global simulation or acquisition settings that do not enter the selected response, especially when their locator contains a branch-specific value incompatible with the other branch.
Preserve operational definitions separately from captions and fitted relations. A readout anchor must cover how the observable is defined; claim anchors must additionally cover the equation, domain, aggregation, and uncertainty convention they assert. For each claim, control_domains must give one separately anchored source-applicability domain for every cited control, preserving whether it is an interval, discrete values, fixed value, symbolic statement, or unreported; never substitute the broader paper-level control domain. For each readout, resolution is either a separately anchored measurement_resolution/reporting_increment object or null when the source supports neither. Do not infer resolution from uncertainty or silently treat decimal formatting as instrument resolution.
When the paper overloads notation or distinguishes a crossing-relative quantity from an absolute one, create separate readouts or claims and record the ambiguity. Never combine their equations or speculate why one presentation differs.
When main text, caption, appendix, or supplement uses materially different definitions or formulas, record the issue in source_ambiguities and do not silently reconcile it. Link every ambiguity to all affected claims, mechanisms, controls, readouts, and fixed conditions; leave all reference arrays empty only when the ambiguity affects the paper globally.
Set case_authoring_ready true only when the extracted evidence can support at least one numeric control, one numeric readout, one quantitative mechanism, and an objective source-grounded response within an explicit domain.
Do not generate Player background, initial observations, episode budgets, diagnostic or hidden conditions, counterfactuals, or code. The claim.oracle_outputs source relation is the only expression tree requested at this extraction stage.

L000040		\begin{abstract}
L000041	We adapt recent ideas for many-body chaos in nonlinear, Hamiltonian fluids
L000042		[Murugan \textit{et al.}, Phys. Rev. Lett. 127, 124501 (2021)] to
L000043		revisit the question of the Reynolds number Re dependence of the Lyapunov exponent $\lambda\propto{\rm Re}^\alpha$
L000044		in fully developed turbulence. The use of such decorrelators
L000045		allow us to investigate
L000046		the interplay of the competing effects of viscous dissipation and nonlinearity. We obtain a precise value of $\alpha = 0.59 \pm 0.04$ and show that departure from the Kolmogorov
L000047			mean field result
L000048		$\lambda \propto \sqrt{{\rm Re}}$ is a consequence of the intermittent fluctuations in the velocity-gradient tensor. The robustness of our
L000049		results are further confirmed in a local, dynamical systems model
L000050		for turbulence.
L000051	\end{abstract}
L000052	
L000053	
L000054	\maketitle
L000055	
L000056	Fully developed, incompressible turbulence is perhaps the most celebrated example of a chaotic
L000057	system. In contrast to other examples of classical, many-body
L000058	systems showing chaotic behaviour, turbulent flows have the distinction of
L000059	being central across natural world.
L000060	Unsurprisingly, therefore,
L000061	physicists working in problems ranging from astrophysics, atmospheric sciences,
L000062	oceanography, and of course fluid dynamics have to factor in the underlying
L000063	chaotic nature of such flows~\cite{Pandit-Pramana-Review}. This ubiquity is not surprising: After all the
L000064	underlying Navier-Stokes equation, in all such systems, lead to solutions which
L000065	are turbulent in the limit of small viscosities commonly seen in most fluids~\cite{Frisch_1995}.
L000066	
L000067	While mathematical and engineering tools remain indispensable, the ideas of
L000068	statistical physics provide the basis for much of our understanding of
L000069	turbulence, especially in its most general form where the flow is homogeneous
L000070	and isotropic. In particular, chaos along with the other fingerprint of fully
L000071	developed turbulence, namely intermittency, and their dependence \textit{inter
L000072	alia} the Reynolds number Re, forms a major challenge in a complete
L000073	understanding of turbulence.
L000074	
L000075	The \textit{degree} of chaos is usually quantified by the (largest) Lyapunov
L000076	exponent $\lambda$ of the flow. By using arguments tracing back to
L000077	Kolmogorov's seminal work from 1941, Ruelle showed that
L000078	$\lambda \propto \sqrt{{\rm Re}}$~\cite{Ruelle}. This result is a consequence of
L000079	associating the (largest) Lyapunov exponent with the inverse of the smallest
L000080	time-scale of the flow  $\tau_\eta \propto 1/\sqrt{{\rm Re}}$, obtained most simply from
L000081	phenomenological arguments, and thence the $\lambda$-scaling.
L000082	More generally, assuming \textit{a} H\"older exponent $h$ characterising the flow,
L000083	it is easy to show $\lambda \propto Re^{\frac{1-h}{1+h}}$~\cite{Vulpiani}; indeed taking the \textit{monofractal},
L000084	Kolmogorov limit~\cite{K41} of a unique $h = 1/3$ recovers the Ruelle scaling.
L000085	
L000086	The result $\lambda \propto \sqrt{{\rm Re}}$ implicitly assumes a unique small length and
L000087	time-scale characteristic of a monofractal flow. However, the observational, experimental,
L000088	and numerical evidence against this is overwhelming. Indeed, a modern
L000089	rationalisation of turbulence rests on the multifractal approach~\cite{Benzi} developed by
L000090	Frisch and Parisi~\cite{Frisch-Parisi}. Adapting this model, which allows for a spread of H\"older
L000091	exponents $h$ in the flow, leads to the revised scaling obtained by Crisanti
L000092	\textit{et al.} $\lambda \propto {\rm Re}^\alpha$, with $\alpha \approx 0.459$~\cite{Vulpiani}.
L000093	
L000094	This scaling exponent $\alpha \lesssim 0.5$ has been challenged in recent years
L000095	with data from different experiments and direct numerical simulations. For
L000096	example, Berera and Ho ~\cite{BereraPRL} have recently reported $\alpha =
L000097	0.53$. This lack of consensus between the theoretical estimate and measurements
L000098	--- as well as the lack of agreement between different
L000099	simulations~\cite{Yamada1987,Vulpiani,BereraPRL,Siddhartha,Boffetta_2017,Mohan_higher,Vassilicos_2023}
L000100	--- suggests that the origins of chaos in turbulence is far from settled.
L000101	
L000102	But is there a way to address the microscopic origin of $\alpha$ from the
L000103	Navier-Stokes equation itself and connect it to the intermittent aspect of
L000104	fully developed turbulence?  And what role does the non-locality (in length
L000105	scale) of interactions --- a defining feature of the Navier-Stokes equation ---
L000106	play?
L000107	
L000108	In this paper we show that this is indeed possible through recently
L000109	constructed ideas of \textit{decorrelators}~\cite{Lightcone} --- largely
L000110	limited to Hamiltonian~\cite{Subhro_PRB,Subhro_PRL,GTEuler} systems in the
L000111	context ergodicity, thermalisation and chaos --- and adapt them for
L000112	driven-dissipative, non-equilibrium systems such as turbulence. Consequently,
L000113	by using a suitable mix of theory and numerical simulations, we uncover the
L000114	competing effects of the viscous and nonlinear terms to show \textit{exactly}
L000115	the chaos and the scaling $\lambda \sim {\rm Re}^\alpha$ emerges along with
L000116	what determining the value of $\alpha = 0.59 \pm 0.04$ and why this
L000117	is so. We also confirm the robustness of this result by using a dynamical
L000118	systems approach to turbulence with the additional advantage of exploiting its
L000119	nearest and next-nearest neighbour interactions to investigate short-time
L000120	effects of locality which are absent in the Navier-Stokes equation.
L000121	
L000122	
L000123	We begin with the three-dimensional, incompressible, unit-density Navier-Stokes equation, driven by an external
L000124	force to a non-equilibrium statistically steady state.
L000125	The force ${\bf f}$ varies to ensure a constant energy injection~\cite{Pope_forcing} $\mathcal{I}
L000126	= \langle {\bf f}\cdot {\bf u} \rangle \equiv \overline{\langle \varepsilon
L000127	\rangle}$, where the mean energy dissipation rate $\overline{\langle \varepsilon
L000128	\rangle}$ is the time $\overline{\cdot \cdot \cdot}$ and space $\langle \cdot
L000129	\cdot \cdot \rangle$ average of the spatio-temporally fluctuating dissipation
L000130	$\varepsilon ({\bf x},t)$ characteristic of such non-equilibrium steady states of fully developed
L000131	turbulence with a statistically steady velocity field ${\bf u}_{\rm
L000132	steady}$. This follows from the familiar, instantaneous (spatially-averaged)
L000133	kinetic energy $E$ balance: $\frac{dE}{dt} = -\langle \varepsilon \rangle +
L000134	\mathcal{I}$ with a mean kinetic energy $E_0 = \overline {E}$.
L000135	
L000136	We now construct two, \textit{nearly} identical,  velocity fields ${\bf u_0}^{\rm A}
L000137	\equiv {\bf u}_{\rm steady}$ and ${\bf u_0}^{\rm B} = {\bf u_0}^{\rm A} +
L000138	\delta {\bf u_0}$, where the form of $\delta {\bf u_0}$ ensures that system B
L000139	remains incompressible.  We choose the amplitude of perturbation $\epsilon_0$
L000140	sufficiently small (see Appendix~\ref{App_DNS}) and localise it in space at ${\bf x}_0$; the precise choice
L000141	of ${\bf x}_0$ is irrelevant and can be chosen to be the center of our domain.
L000142	
L000143	We choose these fields ---  ${\bf u_0}^{\rm A}$ and  ${\bf u_0}^{\rm B}$ --- as
L000144	initial conditions $t = 0$ for the Navier-Stokes equation, evolve them independently in time, and
L000145	calculate the velocity difference $\delta {\bf u} ({\bf x},t) \equiv  {\bf
L000146	u}^{\rm B}({\bf x},t) - {\bf u}^{\rm A}({\bf x},t)$ for $t > 0$. From such
L000147	velocity differences, we are able to construct the decorrelator $\phi({\bf
L000148	x},t) \equiv \frac{1}{2} |\delta {\bf u} ({\bf x},t)|^2 $~\cite{GTEuler,mukherjee2023intermittency}.
L000149	It is easy to show, starting from the Navier-Stokes equation written separately for systems A and
L000150	B, that the decorrelator follows an evolution (written in component form and
L000151	sum over repeated indices assumed)
L000152	\begin{equation}

L000458	\subsection{The Navier-Stokes Equation}
L000459	
L000460	We perform direct numerical simulations (DNSs), by using a pseudospectral method, of the three-dimensional (3D),
L000461	incompressible, unit density Navier Stokes equation, with the pressure field $P$
L000462	\begin{equation}
L000463		\frac{\partial {\bf u}}{\partial t} + {\bf u}\cdot\nabla {\bf u} = \nu \nabla^2 {\bf u} - \nabla P + {\bf f}.
L000464	\label{eq:NS}
L000465	\end{equation}
L000466	on a periodic box of size $L = 2\pi$ with $N^3$ collocation points. We choose $N = 256$ and $N = 512$ (to check for numerical
L000467	convergence) and vary the coefficient viscosity $10^{-3}\le \nu \le 32\times10^{-3}$ to obtain Reynolds numbers $ 50 \le {\rm Re} \le 1400 $.
L000468	We use a second-order
L000469	Adams-Bashforth for time-marching with a time step $\delta t = 5  \times 10^{-4} $ (for $N = 256$) and
L000470	$\delta t = 4\times 10^{-4} \ $ (for $N = 512$).
L000471	
L000472	We initialise the flow with a random initial condition such that the
L000473	initial energy spectrum spectrum $E(k) = A_0 k^2 \exp(-k^2 / 2k_0^2)$ with $A_0
L000474	= k_0 = 1$. The system is driven to a non-equilibrium steady state (NESS)
L000475	through a large-scale forcing with a constant energy injection at large scales
L000476	corresponding to wavenumber $1 \le k_{\rm force}\le 2$.
L000477	
L000478	This statistically steady velocity field ${\bf u}$ is taken as the initial field for system A: ${\bf u_0}^{\rm A}
L000479	\equiv {\bf u}$ and further define the initial condition for system B via ${\bf u_0}^{\rm B} = {\bf u_0}^{\rm A} +
L000480	\delta {\bf u_0}$. We use a Gaussian perturbation
L000481	$\delta {\bf u}_0 ({\bf x}) = \epsilon_0 \exp{(-(x - x_0)^2 / 2\sigma_0^2)}{\bf \hat{x}}$ with $\epsilon_0 = 10^{-5}$, $\sigma_0=4{\rm d}x $ and $x_0 = ({\pi, \pi, \pi})$ at the center of the domain and which also satisfies the incompressibility constraint.
L000482	
L000483	The nearly identical fields  ${\bf u_0}^{\rm A}$ and  ${\bf u_0}^{\rm B}$ are then used as initial conditions for the Navier-Stokes
L000484	equation and evolved as before.
L000485	The decorrelator is calculated from the evolution of such twin simulations as
L000486	$\phi({\bf x},t) = |{\bf u}^{\rm B} - {\bf u}^{\rm A}|^2/2$ and thence $\Phi(t) = \int d{\bf x} \phi({\bf x},t) / \mathcal{V}$.
L000487	The decorrelators are then used to estimate the Lyapunov exponents (obtained by fitting the initial exponential growth phase)
L000488	and its dependence on the Reynolds number.
L000489	
L000490	\subsection{The Gledzer-Ohkitani-Yamada (GOY) Model}
L000491	The Gledzer-Ohkitani-Yamada or the GOY shell model
L000492	\begin{eqnarray}
L000493		\frac{d}{dt} u_n &=& \iota k_n [u_{n+2}u_{n+1} - \frac{1}{4}u_{n+1}u_{n-1}
L000494		- \frac{1}{8} u_{n-1}u_{n-2}]^* \nonumber \\ &-& \nu k_n^2 u_n + f
L000495		\label{eq:GOY}
L000496	\end{eqnarray}
L000497	is one of several cascade models which mimic Navier-Stokes turbulence and are designed to achieve
L000498	very high Reynolds number.
L000499	In such models, the velocities $u_n$ (with boundary conditions $u_{-1} =
L000500	u_{0} = u_{N+1} = u_{N+2} = 0$)  associated with a scalar, exponentially
L000501	growing, wave-number $k_n = k_0 2^n$, are complex, dynamical
L000502	variables. The shell numbers range from $1 \le n \le N$; in our simulations we
L000503	choose $N = 22$ and the coefficient of viscosity varies as $2\times 10^{-7} \le
L000504	\nu \le 64 \times 10^{-7}$ yielding Reynolds numbers in the range $ 8.7 \times 10^6
L000505	 \le {\rm Re}
L000506	\le 2.6 \times 10^8$; the shell model,
L000507	Reynolds number is simply defined as ${\rm Re} = |u_{\rm rms}|/k_0\nu$.
L000508	The equation is integrated numerically by using a second-order Runge-Kutta scheme with a time step $\delta t = 2 \times 10^{-5}$
L000509	The constant amplitude forcing $f = 0.1$, applied on the $n = 2$  shell and drives the system to a statistically steady
L000510	state~\cite{Ray2008}.
L000511	
L000512	As with the strategy for the Navier-Stokes equation, we first obtain a non-equilibrium statistically steady
L000513	state with  an energy spectrum $E(k_n) \equiv |u_n|^2/k_n \sim k_n^{-5/3}$ over an inertial range
L000514	of shells whose extent is determined by Re. We use this steady state velocity field to define the initial
L000515	field for system A --- $u_{n,0}^{\rm A}$ and construct the initial condition for system B via
L000516	$u^B_{n,0} = (1 + \epsilon_0)
L000517	\delta_{n,n_p} u_{n,0}^A$. In all our simulations we have used $\epsilon_0 =
L000518	0.001$ and $n_p = 16$.  Numerically it has been seen that the shell wise
L000519	decorrelators first show an power-law rise later followed by the
L000520	exponential-{growth}
L000521	regime. The initial power law largely depends on the
L000522	distance from the perturbed shell. Therefore, we add the perturbation in a fixed
L000523	shell $n_p = 16$ for all values of ${\rm Re}$.

L000529	\section{Derivation of the decorrelator from the Navier-Stokes equation and its limits} \label{Phi_derivation}
L000530	\renewcommand{\theequation}{B-\arabic{equation}}
L000531	\setcounter{equation}{0}
L000532	\subsection{Evolution equation for $\phi({\bf r},t)$ and $\Phi$}
L000533	In this section we provide the derivation of the equation of motion of the decorrelator for the Navier-Stokes equation and
L000534	in particular estimate the long and short time limits of $\beta_S$ and $\beta_\eta$.
L000535	
L000536	We begin by recalling that the pressure term in the Navier-Stokes equation can be rewritten as a Poisson equation
L000537	\begin{equation}
L000538	\nabla^2 P = - {\partial_j u_i}{\partial_i u_j}
L000539	\end{equation}
L000540	by exploiting the incompressibility constraint. This Poisson equation underlines the non-local nature of turbulence.
L000541	
L000542	It is useful, in what follows, to have a Green's function representation
L000543	\begin{equation}
L000544		P({\bf x}) = -\int {\rm d}{\bf x} G({\bf x},{\bf x}^\prime)
L000545		\left [{\partial_j u_i}{\partial_i u_j}\right ]^\prime
L000546	\end{equation}
L000547		where the $\prime$ denotes the quantity evaluated at ${\bf x}^\prime$.
L000548	
L000549	This allows us to construct the
L000550	evolution equation of the solenoidal
L000551	velocity perturbation $\delta {\bf u} = {\bf u}^{\rm B} - {\bf u}^{\rm A}$ in component form
L000552	\begin{equation}
L000553	\frac{\partial \delta u_i}{\partial t} = - \delta u_j \partial_j u_i^{\rm A} - u_j^{\rm B} \partial_j \delta u_i
L000554	-  \partial_i \left(\int {\rm d}{\bf x}
L000555	G({\bf x},{\bf x'}) [\partial^2_{jk} (u_j^{\rm A}\delta u_k +\delta u_j u_k^{\rm A} + \delta u_j\delta u_k)]'\right) + \nu \nabla^2 \delta u_i + \delta u_i \delta f_{i}
L000556	\label{delu}
L000557	\end{equation}
L000558	and hence, via a dot product of  $\delta {\bf u}$ with Eq.~\eqref{delu}, the equation for
L000559	the decorrelator $\phi ({\bf r},t)$:
L000560	\begin{equation}
L000561	\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial t} = - \delta u_i S_{ij} \delta u_j
L000562	-  \partial_i W_i + \nu \delta u _i\nabla^2 \delta u_i + \delta u_i \delta f_{i}.
L000563	\label{phi_resolved}
L000564	\end{equation}
L000565	Here, $S_{ij} = \frac{1}{2}  (\partial_j u_i^{\rm A} + \partial_i u_j^{\rm A})$ is the strain-rate tensor
L000566	and $W_i = u_i^{\rm B} \phi + \delta u_i\int {\rm d}{\bf x}
L000567	G({\bf x},{\bf x'}) [\partial^2_{jk} (u_j^{\rm A}\delta u_k +\delta u_j u_k^{\rm A} + \delta u_j\delta u_k)]'$.
L000568	
L000569	A spatial integration with $\Phi = \int d{\bf x} \phi$ now leads to the cancellation of the divergence term and hence
L000570	\begin{equation}
L000571	\frac{d\Phi}{dt} = - \langle \delta u_i S_{ij} \delta u_j\rangle +\nu \langle \delta u_i \nabla^2 \delta u_i \rangle + \langle \delta u_i \delta f_i\rangle \equiv \beta_S + \beta_\eta + \langle \delta u_i \delta f_i\rangle
L000572	\end{equation}
L000573	the evolution equation for our spatially integrated decorrelator as discussed in the main text of the manuscript.
L000574	
L000575	
L000576	
L000577	
L000578

L000580	\subsection{Short and long-time asymptotics of $\beta_S$}
L000581	At early times, $\langle \delta u_i \delta f_i\rangle = 0$ (since the forcing terms are nearly identical), the pre saturation exponential growth of the decorrelator with the Lyapunov exponent $\lambda = \lambda^{\rm DNS} \sim \lambda_S$
L000582	is controlled by the short time asymptotics of $\beta_S$. Hence, in what follows, we drop the contribution from
L000583	$\beta_\eta$, to simplify notation.
L000584	
L000585	We now expand  $\delta u_i S_{ij} \delta u_j$ in the eigenbasis of the strain-rate tensor, with eigenvalues
L000586	$\gamma_i$ and direction cosines $\cos\theta_i$, to obtain
L000587	\begin{equation}
L000588		\frac{\partial}{\partial t} \phi = - \phi({\bf x},t)\, \Gamma({\bf x},t)
L000589		\label{eq:beta_S}
L000590	\end{equation}
L000591	with
L000592	$\Gamma({\bf x},t) \equiv \left(\sum_{i=1}^{3} \gamma_i({\bf x}, t) \cos^2\theta_i({\bf x}, t)\right)
L000593	\approx \gamma_3({\bf x}, t) \cos^2\theta_3({\bf x}, t)$ dominated by the compressional eigendirection
L000594	as discussed in the main text.
L000595	
L000596	We choose an integrating factor  $e^{\Theta({\bf x}, t)}$, such that
L000597	$\partial_t \Theta({\bf x}, t) = \Gamma({\bf x}, t)$, to obtain the form of the spatially-resolved decorrator
L000598	at time $t$
L000599	\begin{equation}
L000600	\phi({\bf x}, t) = \phi({\bf x}, 0) e^{\Theta({\bf x}, 0) -\Theta({\bf x}, t)}
L000601		\label{eq:IF}
L000602	\end{equation}
L000603	
L000604	We are now able to spatially integrate Eq.~\eqref{eq:IF} and, keeping in mind that the initially localised perturbation
L000605	$\phi({\bf x}, 0)$ is independent of $e^{\Theta({\bf x}, 0) -\Theta({\bf x}, t)}$, we obtain
L000606	\begin{equation}
L000607	\Phi(t) = \Phi(0) \langle e^{\Theta({\bf x}, 0) -\Theta({\bf x}, t)} \rangle
L000608		\label{eq:IF-int}
L000609	\end{equation}
L000610	where the angular brackets $\langle \cdot \cdot \rangle \equiv \int d{\bf x} (\cdot \cdot)$.
L000611	
L000612	Since we are interested in the short-time asymptotics of $\beta_S$, it is possible to Taylor expand
L000613	the exponential and, keeping in mind the mapping of $\Theta$ to $\Gamma$, we obtain
L000614	\begin{equation}
L000615	\Phi(t) \lesssim \Phi(0) \exp \left[ \sum_{p = 1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^p}{p!} \langle \Delta \Theta({\bf x}, t)^p\rangle \right]
L000616		\label{eq:exp}
L000617	\end{equation}
L000618	where $\Delta \Theta({\bf x}, t) = \Theta({\bf x}, t) - \Theta({\bf x}, 0)$.
L000619	Considering terms up to $\mathcal{O}(\Delta \Theta^2)$, to account for corrections stemming from intermittent
L000620	fluctuations~\cite{BereraPRL},
L000621	\begin{equation}
L000622	\Phi(t) \lesssim \Phi(0) \exp \left [- \langle \Delta \Theta \rangle + \frac{1}{2}\langle \Delta \Theta^2\rangle \right ]
L000623		\label{eq:2ndorder}
L000624	\end{equation}
L000625	
L000626	Now all that remains is the evaluation of $\langle \Delta \Theta \rangle$ and $\langle \Delta \Theta^2\rangle$.
L000627	
L000628	From the choice of $\Theta$ it is easy to see (by interchanging time and space integrals
L000629	$\langle \cdot \cdot \rangle \equiv \int d{\bf x} (\cdot \cdot)$ suitably) that $\langle \Delta \Theta \rangle \propto \langle \gamma_3 \rangle \sim  \sqrt{{\rm Re}}$ (see Fig. 4 of the main text). The determination of $\langle \Delta \Theta^2\rangle$
L000630	requires a further Ansatz of an approximate delta-correlation in time, at least over time-scales of the order
L000631	associated with strain-rate,
L000632	to yield  $\langle \Delta \Theta^2\rangle \propto \gamma_3^{\rm std} \sim {\rm Re}^{0.59}$ (see Fig. 4
L000633	of the main text as well as Fig.~\ref{3fig}(c) which shows that indeed the distribution of
L000634	$\gamma_3$ changes with Re) which, in the large Reynolds number limit dominates over the  $\sqrt{{\rm Re}}$ of the mean exponent.
L000635	Hence $\lambda = \lambda^{\rm DNS} \sim \lambda_S \sim {\rm Re}^\alpha$ with $\alpha = 0.59 \pm 0.04$.
L000636	
L000637	
L000638	This then completes the proof of how the intermittency induced fluctuations determines the Lyapunov exponent
L000639	for fully-developed turbulence.
L000640	
L000641	
L000642	At long times, beyond the exponential-growth phase when the systems have
L000643	started to completely decorrelate the forcing term can not be neglected.  Thus
L000644	as $t \to \infty$, we estimate   $\langle \delta u_i \delta f_i \rangle =
L000645	\langle u^B_i f^B_i \rangle + \langle u^A_i f^A_i \rangle - \langle (u^B_i
L000646	f^A_i + u^A_i f^B_i) \rangle \to 2\overline{\langle \varepsilon\rangle}$. As we
L000647	shall see below, this exactly compensates the contribution of the viscous term
L000648	$\beta_\eta$ at long times.
L000649	
L000650	
L000651	
L000652	
L000653	
L000654	\subsection{Short and long-time asymptotics of $\beta_\eta$}
L000655	
L000656	The viscous term can be expanded as
L000657	\begin{eqnarray}
L000658	\beta_\eta &=& \nu\langle \delta u_i \nabla^2 \delta u_i \rangle = - \nu\langle \partial_j \delta u_i \partial_j \delta u_i\rangle \nonumber\\
L000659	&=& -\nu \langle(\partial_i u_j^B \partial_i u^B_j + \partial_i u_j^A \partial_i u^A_j - 2\partial_i u_j^B \partial_i u^A_j) \rangle \nonumber\\
L000660	&=& - 4\nu \operatorname{Tr}(S^2) + 2 \nu \langle \partial_i u_j^{\rm A} \partial_i u_j^{\rm B}\rangle = 2\langle \varepsilon\rangle + 2 \nu \langle \partial_i u_j^{\rm A} \partial_i u_j^{\rm B}\rangle.
L000661	\end{eqnarray}
L000662	
L000663	We find at short times, in the exponential-growth phase,
L000664	this terms scales as $\beta_\eta =  \mathcal{O}(1/\tau_\eta)$,
L000665	where $\tau_\eta = \sqrt{\frac{\nu}{\overline{\langle
L000666	\varepsilon\rangle} }}$ corresponds to the smallest Kolmogorov time scales.
L000667	However, at long times $t \to \infty$, systems A and B decorrelate leading to
L000668	$\langle \partial_i u_j^{\rm A} \partial_i u_j^{\rm B}\rangle \to 0$ and hence
L000669	$\beta_\eta \sim -2\langle\varepsilon\rangle$ (see Fig.~\ref{3fig}(a) as well as the main text).
L000670	This is easily understandable because, on average, dissipation is balanced by the energy injection derived above.
L000671

L000696	\section{Decorrelator in the shell model for turbulence} \label{App_shell}
L000697	\renewcommand{\theequation}{C-\arabic{equation}}
L000698	\setcounter{equation}{0}
L000699	It is possible to construct an evolution equation for the decorrelator in our shell model but, as we shall see, its structure is
L000700	less transparent than what we have seen for the Navier-Stokes equation.
L000701	
L000702	By subtracting the GOY model equations for systems A and B we obtain
L000703	the evolution of the shell-by-shell  velocity difference $\delta u_n = u_n^{\rm B} - u_n^{\rm A}$:
L000704	\begin{eqnarray}
L000705	    \frac{d}{dt} \delta u_n
L000706	    &=& \iota k_n [(\delta u_{n+2}u^{\rm A}_{n+1} + \delta u_{n+2}u^{\rm A}_{n+1} + \delta u_{n+2}\delta u_{n+1}) - \frac{\epsilon}{\lambda}(\delta u_{n+1}u^{\rm A}_{n-1} + \delta u_{n+1}u^{\rm A}_{n-1} + \delta u_{n+1}\delta u_{n-1})  \nonumber \\
L000707	    &+& \frac{(\epsilon - 1)}{\lambda^2} (\delta u_{n-2}u^{\rm A}_{n-1} + \delta u_{n-2}u^{\rm A}_{n-1} + \delta u_{n-2}\delta u_{n-1})]^* - \nu k_n^2 \delta u_n.
L000708	\label{shell_diff}
L000709	\end{eqnarray}
L000710	From this by suitably multiplying with the complex conjugate field $\delta u^*$, the decorrlator obeys
L000711	
L000712	\begin{eqnarray}
L000713	\frac{d}{dt} \phi_n &=& \frac{\iota k_n}{2} [(\delta u_{n+2}u^{\rm A}_{n+1}\delta u_{n} + \delta u_{n+2}u^{\rm A}_{n+1}\delta u_{n} + \delta u_{n+2}\delta u_{n+1}\delta u_{n}) - \frac{\epsilon}{\lambda}(\delta u_{n+1}\delta u_{n}u^{\rm A}_{n-1} + \delta u_{n+1}\delta u_{n}u^{\rm A}_{n-1} \nonumber\\
L000714	&+& \delta u_{n+1}\delta u_{n}\delta u_{n-1}) + \frac{(\epsilon - 1)}{\lambda^2} (\delta u_{n-2}u^{\rm A}_{n-1}\delta u_{n} + \delta u_{n-2}u^{\rm A}_{n-1}\delta u_{n} + \delta u_{n-2}\delta u_{n-1}\delta u_{n})]^* + c.c. - 2\nu k_n^2 \phi_n.
L000715	\label{shell_phi}
L000716	\end{eqnarray}
L000717	A summation over all shells leads to simplifications in the evolution of the GOY model decorrelator $\Phi^{\rm GOY}$
L000718	\begin{eqnarray}
L000719		\frac{d}{dt}\Phi^{\rm GOY} &=& \frac{\iota}{2} \sum k_n [\epsilon\delta u_{n} u^{\rm A}_{n+1}\delta u _{n+2} + (1-\epsilon)\delta u_{n} \delta u_{n+1}u^{\rm A} _{n+2} - u^{\rm A}_{n} \delta u_{n+1}\delta u _{n+2}]^* + c.c - 2\nu \sum_n k_n^2 \phi_n
L000720	\end{eqnarray}
L000721	
L000722	Further progress is only possible through a numerical solution of the
L000723	decorrelator equation as we report in the main text of the manuscript. The
L000724	shell-wise decorrelator at very short times show a power-law growth with a
L000725	wavenumber-dependent scaling exponent.  In particular at long times when the
L000726	decorrelator saturates, we find, unsurprisingly, $|\delta u_n|^2 \sim |u_n|^2
L000727	\sim k_n^{-2/3}$ as shown in Fig.~\ref{3fig}(d).
